call sit four layers: rclcpp, the C++ library; rcl, a C library holding what every client library shares; rmw, a small interface of C functions such as

; and one package per vendor implementing that interface on an actual DDS library. Everything above rmw is written against those functions, never a vendor, which lets you swap the vendor at start-up, with an environment variable, and recompile nothing. DDS itself has no broker and no master: every process announces itself and finds the others.
The problem this layering solves is letting nodes find each other and exchange data without wiring the code to one transport, and without a single process whose failure takes the graph down.

Discovery happens in two stages. Participants announce themselves over multicast first, so a process starting late still finds the ones already running; then participants that found each other exchange their topics, types and QoS profiles over unicast, which is why another process's QoS settings can be read from the command line at all. A domain id splits one network into logical ones through port numbers alone, a fixed block per domain and a smaller one per participant, so two domain ids sharing a cable never see each other's announcements. A process holds exactly one participant however many nodes it contains, since a process normally has one context, so participant count, not node count, is what discovery traffic and port use scale with.

The mistake under pressure is treating a silent graph as a node problem. Two machines can ping and ssh each other while discovering nothing, because discovery depends on UDP multicast on ports that have nothing to do with basic reachability: a different domain id, a different middleware vendor, a client-isolated Wi-Fi access point, a managed switch, or two subnets each stop discovery outright, with no error on either side, only an empty topic list. Discovering a node also is not talking to it: two nodes that find each other can still refuse every message over incompatible delivery promises, a separate question.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: naming all four layers under a publish call, saying how the same compiled node runs on a different DDS vendor with no rebuild, explaining what a domain id changes on the wire, and getting the participant count right for a process holding several nodes: one, not one per node.

DDS itself is an OMG standard for data-centric publish and subscribe, and RTPS, properly DDSI-RTPS, is its wire protocol. The property that matters most to ROS 2 is that it has no broker and no master. Every process announces itself and finds the others, which is why killing one node never takes the graph down, and also why a node that nobody can discover fails silently instead of getting an error.

happens in two stages. First, participant discovery: each participant sends an announcement to a well-known multicast address and port, and repeats it, so that a participant starting later still finds the ones already running. Second, endpoint discovery: two participants that have found each other exchange the list of their publishers and subscriptions over unicast, with each one's topic name, type name, type hash and full QoS profile. Matching happens per pair and per topic, in both processes independently. That exchange is why
can print another process's QoS profile, and why a QoS mismatch is decided at discovery time rather than at publish time.

The domain id is how DDS splits one physical network into logical ones, and it does that entirely through port numbers. The RTPS specification computes the ports from a base of 7400, a 250-port block per domain, and 2 ports per participant inside that block. The ROS 2 documentation on the domain id gives the constants and the worked examples, and the program in the worked example below computes them. Three consequences follow, and all three show up in real systems:

items.v: Two groups on different domain ids share a cable and never see each other. This is the cheapest isolation there is, and the first thing to check when nothing is discovered.

The highest id whose ports still fit in a 16-bit port number is 232. On Linux the default ephemeral range, 32768 to 60999, sits in the middle of that span, so the ids clear of it are 0 to 101 and 215 to 232. Pick from the lower block unless you have a reason not to.
A domain's block is only 250 ports wide, so the 121st process on one computer in domain 1 lands on domain 2's multicast ports.

c.v: are the unit that all of this counts. One participant belongs to one

, and a process has one context unless you make more, so a process has one participant however many nodes you put in it. The Jazzy page on the domain id states it plainly: for each ROS 2 process running on a computer, one DDS participant is created. Each participant costs two ports, its own share of the announcement traffic, and its own copy of the discovery database, which holds an entry for every endpoint in the domain. Twenty single-node processes on a robot means twenty participants and a discovery database replicated twenty times; twenty nodes in one component container means one participant. That is the argument for composition that has nothing to do with copying messages.

Across machines, the list of things that break is short and always the same. The two ends are on different domain ids or different rmw implementations. One end has

. Multicast is dropped, by client isolation on a Wi-Fi access point, by a managed switch, or by a firewall that lets ping through and not UDP 7400 and up. The two ends are on different subnets, so announcements are never routed. A VPN or a docker bridge carries the announcements out of the interface you meant. And once data does flow, a large message over Wi-Fi meets IP fragmentation: one lost fragment leaves the rest in the kernel's reassembly buffer, which defaults to 256 KB, until
expires after 30 seconds, and during that time nothing else gets in. The link looks fine and the topic hangs.
Here is the port arithmetic, written out. Give it a domain id and a participant index and it says which four UDP ports that participant uses:

blocks.text:
domain   0, participant   0: multicast 7400 7401, unicast 7410 7411
domain   1, participant   0: multicast 7650 7651, unicast 7660 7661
domain   1, participant 119: multicast 7650 7651, unicast 7898 7899
domain   1, participant 120: multicast 7650 7651, unicast 7900 7901  <- on top of the next domain
domain   2, participant   0: multicast 7900 7901, unicast 7910 7911
domain 101, participant  54: multicast 32650 32651, unicast 32768 32769  <- inside the ephemeral range

c.v: Read the rows in pairs. Domain 0 and domain 1 have no port in common, which is the whole isolation mechanism, and it is also why a firewall rule written for domain 0 silently blocks nothing when somebody moves the robot to domain 7. Domain 1's 121st participant, index 120, takes 7900 and 7901 for its own unicast traffic, and those are domain 2's multicast ports: two groups that believed they were separate now collide. And on Linux, domain 101 runs out of room after 54 participants, because the next pair of ports is inside the range the kernel hands out to anything that opens a socket.

The same arithmetic tells you what to open on a firewall. For domain 5 with at most 20 processes per machine, you need UDP 8650 and 8651 for multicast and UDP 8660 to 8699 for unicast, and nothing else.
